summary: This informational RFC specifies an automated policy for border routers deciding how to handle Admin-Local scope multicast messages sent with the Multicast Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks. The goal is to avoid manual configuration when deciding which such messages should cross the border.

plainLanguage.summary: A gate guard needs a rule for which messages may leave a neighborhood. This gives the guard a rule it can follow automatically without someone setting it up by hand.

questions: how does mpl detect mesh boundaries
subtitle: Automatic policy for routing multicast messages within site boundaries.

tldr.problem: Border routers connecting mesh networks need to know which Admin-Local scope multicast messages should cross from one network to another, but administrative configuration is cumbersome.
tldr.mechanism: The MPL4 router automatically detects MPL-enabled interfaces on connected links by sending probe messages and recording responses, then forwards Admin-Local multicast messages only over interfaces that have responded.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can interconnect multiple mesh networks without manual configuration of which multicast messages propagate across the boundaries.

facts.label: Mesh technologies supported
facts.value: IEEE 802.15.4, IEEE 802.11, ITU-T G.9959, Bluetooth Low Energy

today: RFC 7732 is an Informational specification published in February 2016. It remains the reference for automated Admin-Local scope multicast policies in MPL border routers.

sections.title: Admin-Local Multicast Routing
sections.content:
Admin-Local scope in IPv6 multicast lets organizations create their own boundaries for message propagation. RFC 7732 specifies an automated policy for border routers that sit between mesh networks running the Multicast Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (MPL). Instead of requiring an administrator to manually configure which interfaces should forward Admin-Local messages, the MPL4 router discovers and maintains this automatically.

The policy builds on autonomous networking principles, allowing networks like Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks (LoWPANs) composed of nodes using IEEE 802.15.4 to interconnect seamlessly with other mesh networks without human intervention.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of someone deciding by hand which doors messages can pass through, the system tests which doors lead to networks that speak the same language, then automatically lets messages through only to those doors.

sections.title: Network Identifiers Across Technologies
sections.content:
Different mesh technologies identify networks differently. An IEEE 802.15.4 LoWPAN identifies networks by PAN ID. IEEE 802.11 uses SSID. ITU-T G.9959 uses HomeID. The RFC maps these technology-specific identifiers to a general concept: a network identifier that marks which interfaces belong together. BLUETOOTH Low Energy has no such concept, so all BTLE interfaces share a network identifier of "any".

When the MPL4 router forwards a message, it compares network identifiers. A message from an 802.15.4 network with PAN ID 100 can only forward to another 802.15.4 interface with the same PAN ID, preventing unintended cross-network propagation.
sections.plainLanguage: Different network types use different names for "which neighborhood am I in". The system knows how to read each type's name tag and matches them correctly.

sections.title: Automatic Zone Detection
sections.content:
The MPL4 router periodically tests each of its interfaces to determine which are truly connected to MPL-enabled neighbors. Every MPL_CHECK_INT seconds (default 5 minutes), it sends a multicast probe message to the special address ALL_MPL_FORWARDERS with Admin-Local scope. When a neighbor receives this probe, it responds by rebroadcasting it. If the probe returns to the originating interface, that interface is marked as part of the MPL4 zone (by setting MPL_BLOCKED to false). If no response arrives within MPL_TO seconds, the interface is marked as blocked.

This continuous probing ensures the router responds to network changes: when a mesh network is suddenly connected, the router discovers it within minutes; when a mesh is disconnected, the router stops forwarding to it within the timeout window.
sections.plainLanguage: Every few minutes, the guard sends a test message to see which neighbors are listening. If the message comes back, that neighbor is connected and messages can go there. If not, the route is closed.

sections.title: Message Forwarding Policy
sections.content:
Once zones are determined, the policy defines what messages the router forwards:

Link-Local and Realm-Local scope messages (scopes 2 and 3) never cross zone boundaries. These are designed for local mesh operation only. Admin-Local scope messages (scope 4) forward to all MPL interfaces that (1) subscribe to the same multicast address, (2) share the same zone index, (3) have PROACTIVE_FORWARDING enabled, and (4) have MPL_BLOCKED set to false (meaning the interface detected active neighbors). Global scope messages (scope 5 and higher) without the MPL header get wrapped in an MPL header and forwarded to All_MPL_FORWARDERS scope 4.

A crucial requirement: incoming messages protected at Layer 2 (encrypted at the link layer) must be re-protected at all outgoing interfaces, using that interface's encryption keys. This allows each mesh network to maintain its own encryption while allowing messages to pass through.
sections.plainLanguage: Local messages stay local. Neighborhood messages go to all detected neighbors. Global messages get wrapped up and sent as neighborhood messages. Every message leaves with the right encryption for its destination neighborhood.

sections.title: Security Trade-offs
sections.content:
The RFC identifies four security scenarios based on two dimensions: whether the source mesh uses Layer 2 encryption and whether the MPL4 router is administratively managed.

In an unmanaged, unencrypted network, any node can send malicious Admin-Local messages over the entire interconnected zone. This is acceptable only for physically isolated networks (like wired office buildings) where node connection is tightly controlled. In a managed, encrypted network, even a malicious node cannot read encrypted messages and cannot forge them; the manager controls which interfaces forward, so the malicious node cannot extend message distribution outside the manager's intended zone. The RFC acknowledges each combination has different risk profiles, and organizations should choose encryption and management appropriate to their threat model and deployment context.
sections.plainLanguage: If messages are locked up (encrypted) and someone checks who gets in (managed), it is safe. If messages are open (unencrypted) and anyone can suggest where they go (unmanaged), it is risky unless the physical space is locked down.

sections.title: Default Parameters
sections.content: Three key parameters control the behavior. MPL_TO defaults to two times DATA_MESSAGE_IMAX, allowing enough time to receive a second response message. MPL_CHECK_INT defaults to 5 minutes, so network changes trigger a response within 5 minutes. MPL_BLOCKED starts as TRUE, meaning interfaces are assumed inactive until they respond to a probe. These defaults balance responsiveness against message overhead and fit the Trickle algorithm intervals used by MPL.
sections.plainLanguage: Three knobs control how fast the system reacts and how much traffic it uses to test neighbors.
